title: Abigail Lewis
text:
Ecosystem ecology, data science, ecological forecasting

Abigail Lewis (she/her) is an ecosystem ecologist and Smithsonian Climate Change Fellow. Her research combines field studies, global data analysis, and ecological forecasting to predict the impacts of global change on aquatic ecosystems. At the Smithsonian Environmental Research Center (SERC), Abby is developing forecasts of methane emission from coastal wetlands to inform marsh restoration and carbon budgeting efforts.
Abby will be starting as a tenure-track professor within the Odum School of Ecology at the University of Georgia in fall of 2027. If you are interested in joining the lab, please see open positions here!

Abigail Lewis, PhD
Biogeochemistry, data science, ecological forecasting











Abigail Lewis is an environmental data scientist and Smithsonian Climate Change Fellow. Her research aims to characterize the effects of climate change on aquatic ecosystems and vice versa—how these changes may feed back to alter the global carbon cycling processes that shape Earth’s climate. At the Smithsonian Environmental Research Center, Abby is developing forecasts of methane emission from wetlands across the coasts of the contiguous United States to inform local and national blue carbon planning efforts.

Outreach
Below are a few examples of recent science outreach efforts:

National Parks Marsh Restoration

I worked with the National Park Service to create a set of communications materials about coastal marsh restoration, including visitor center display boards and digital StoryMaps. This work was done through a science communication fellowship from the Ecological Society of America.

Flipped Science Fair
In our flipped science fair, we gave kids the power to judge graduate student science fair posters. Kids interacted with 27 graduate student presenters in small group settings, and they had the opportunity to see themselves as valued contributors in science. Meanwhile, graduate students had got training and feedback in science communication. We published a paper about the first year of this project here.




  


Stream box
When the COVID-19 pandemic cancelled all in-person science outreach, I worked the New River Land Trust and the Virginia Tech Stream Team to put together a “Stream Box” filled with information and activities that families could use to independently learn about a local stream. The Global Change Center wrote an article about this work here.




  


GirlsLaunch!
GirlsLaunch! is a program at Virginia Tech that aims to combat gender biases by exposing kindergarten-aged children to female scientists. With funding from the Virginia Tech Center for Communicating Science, I developed a video and interactive worksheet activity for the GirlsLaunch! program.







Envirobites
Envirobites works to make environmental research accessible to non-experts. I have written many articles for the site, each of which takes a specific paper and breaks down the key findings.

title: Teaching and Outreach
text:
Teaching
Through my teaching, I aim to empower students with the skills, confidence, and critical thinking necessary to navigate a rapidly changing world.
Previous courses include:


Data Science Skills Series at the Smithsonian Environmental Research Center (summer 2025)



I developed and co-led a series of six data science training workshops for the SERC community, with topics including Git/GitHub, spatial data analysis, and advanced data visualization.



Advanced R Programming at Virginia Tech (co-instructor of record; spring 2023)



I designed and taught a graduate seminar on advanced programming in R (13 students) to help students better leverage computational approaches in their research.

Ecological forecasting
Can we forecast ecology like we forecast the weather? Ecological forecasts are transformative for environmental management because they allow us to prepare for environmental threats before they happen. However, some ecological variables seem to be more predictable than others. I am working to understand where and when forecasts succeed vs. fail so we can make better predictions in the future.

title: Join the lab!
text:
I am planning to hire 1-2 motivated graduate students to start in the fall of 2027. Graduate students will be based in the Odum School of Ecology at UGA, and will be fully funded off of a combination of research and teaching assistantships.

Projects
Potential projects could include:



Automated flux chambers at SERC




Analyzing “hot moments” of methane emission from coastal wetlands. For this project, you would work with a fantastic team of researchers, a state-of-the art mesocosm facility, and an in situ warming experiment at the Smithsonian Environmental Research Center (SERC).



I am hoping to hire one student to lead the mesocosm experiments for this project and potentially also a second student to lead modeling and forecasting efforts.



Analyzing the variability and predictability of water quality in lakes, ponds, and reservoirs. This project would involve fieldwork to set up and monitor an exciting new network of water quality sensors, as well as the opportunity to lead global analyses through the Global Lake Ecological Observatory Network (GLEON).



Lake Agnes (Minnesota, USA)




Forecasting changes in greenhouse gas dynamics across lakes worldwide. This project would include close collaboration with international research teams in the GLEON and the Ecological Forecasting Initiative, with a goal of improving the representation of lakes in the global carbon budget.


There may be opportunities to explore projects beyond those listed above. See Current Research for an overview of active research areas.




The Odum School of Ecology
The Odum School of Ecology is an exciting and unique place to do this research. Because the whole School is dedicated to ecology, you will be surrounded by a large community of like-minded students and faculty, with lots of relevant talks, courses, and other opportunities.
This is a particularly exciting time to be here, as Odum just hired four (!!) new ecosystem ecologists. Three of them are starting in 2026, and I will join in fall 2027. I am really thrilled about the opportunity to collaborate and build a research community with this group. As a student, this means that you will have access to lots of new equipment, relevant courses, reading groups, and faculty (e.g., committee members) to help support your work.
At UGA, you will also have the opportunity to interact and collaborate with other programs and field sites, including the fantastic River Basin Center, which helps connect freshwater science to management and policy.

Aquatic carbon cycling



Water level management dramatically affected carbon cycling processes. Read more in JGR Biogeosciences


Aquatic ecosystems play an important role in the global carbon cycling processes that regulate Earth’s climate. However, anthropogenic changes can modulate the way these ecosystems process carbon, leading to positive or negative climate feedback effects. I use experiments and monitoring to analyze the effects of anthropogenic drivers on the biogeochemistry of carbon in aquatic environments.
